Notes: First documented Jewish presence in the town itself: P.Polit.Iud. 17, letter dated 27th year (of Ptolemy VIII) 1 Tybi = 144/3 BCE. It mentions 'the politarches Euphranor and the archontes', the earliest dated document of the archive of the Jewish politeuma of Herakleopolis (20 papyri from mummy cartonnage, dated 144/3-133/2 BCE; ed. Cowey & Maresch 2001). Basis for Year Established. Not used for Year Established: P.Hib. I 96 (= CPJ I 18), c. 260 BCE, a contract between Andronikos and Alexander son of Andronikos, 'Ioudaios'. Kreuzer (n. 6) cites it as the earliest known document of Jewish presence. It is a Hibeh papyrus and is not explicitly from the city itself, so it is mentioned here only. Also not used: 2nd/1st-c. BCE stelae from a Jewish cemetery at Sedment, 7 km from Herakleopolis, outside the town. Presence only; no count.

c. 139 BCE (midpoint of the archive, 144/3-133/2 BCE, reign of Ptolemy VIII). Kreuzer (2023), following Cowey & Maresch p. 12: 'A high number of Jews lived and worked there, especially in the area of the harbor, and many also may have served at the fortress.' He describes the town as 'small to middle sized'. The community formed a politeuma under an annually elected politarches and archontes, with hyperetai (court officers), a jail and scribes. Its jurisdiction extended to Jewish village communities with presbyteroi (Onnes, Peempasbytis, Tebetnoi, Penei; also Teis in the Oxyrhynchite nome). The archive lists 52 personal names, mostly Greek, including Iakoubis and Iona. Organized community; no numeric estimate given.

P.Polit.Iud. 1, dated 7 October 135 BCE (year 36, 12 Thoth): petition of Andronikos, a member of the politeuma, to the politarches Alexandros and the politeuma of Judeans. It concerns an insult in the street by Nikarchos, 'from the harbor'. Members are called politai and non-Judeans allophyloi. Presence of an organized Jewish politeuma; no count.

P.Polit.Iud. 4, dated 36th year 19 Choiak (= 134 BCE): petition to the archontes by Philotas son of Philotas, a member of the politeuma. Lysimachos had given his betrothed Nikaia to another man without the 'book of separation' (cf. LXX Deut 24:1), and the petitioner asks the archontes to write 'to the Jews in the village'. This is evidence of Jewish marriage custom in the community. Presence only.

P.Polit.Iud. 8, dated 15 March 133 BCE (year 37): petition of Theodotos son of Theodotos, a Jew of Teis (Oxyrhynchite nome), to 'the archontes of the politeuma of the Jews in Herakleopolis' about a loan to the Jewess Plousia and her son Dorotheos. The archontes order a letter 'to the Jews in Teis'. Presence; no count.

Latest dated documents of the archive: the 38th year of Ptolemy VIII (133/2 BCE). They include P.Polit.Iud. 11, a petition of Ptolemaios son of Simon, Jew, against Arsame of the harbour inhabitants, and P.Polit.Iud. 9, Berenike daughter of Archagathos, Jew. After this year the archive gives no further documentation; this is not evidence of the community's end. Presence only.

c. 139 BCE (archive 144/3-133/2 BCE). Honigman (SCI 21, 2002), review of Cowey & Maresch: the archontes' jurisdiction extended to the non-Jewish population of the harbour area, and 'At the very least, the harbour area must have been heavily populated by Jews (p. 12)'. She argues that 'The Jews who belonged to the politeuma in Heracleopolis formed a military settlement, probably including soldiers and wives', with wives and children possibly members of the wider local Jewish community but not of the politeuma. She links the settlement to the fortress near the harbour, which was strategically important in the 2nd c. BCE. Four Jewish village communities appear under presbyteroi. Substantial community; no count.

c. 139 BCE (archive 144/3-133/2 BCE). Ritter (SCI 30, 2011) reads the evidence differently: 'Heracleopolis was home to a board of Jewish archons who received complaints from Jews throughout the entire Heracleopolitan nome', with Jewish elders in many villages and in Teis (Oxyrhynchite nome). He argues the politeuma was the civic body of Heracleopolis, not a Jewish association, while the Jewish archons governed local Jews. Presence of an organized Jewish community; no count.

c. 139 BCE (archive 144/3-133/2 BCE). Sänger (Symposion paper): P.Polit.Iud. documents a Jewish community ('jüdische Gemeinde') resident in Herakleopolis, capital of the Herakleopolite nome, organized as a politeuma. It is documented in the harbour quarter shortly after the phrourarch Dioskoros (P.Phrur.Diosk., 154-145 BCE?) commanded the fortress newly built there in the mid-2nd c. BCE. All petitions in the archive come from Jews, members of the politeuma or not. Presence; no count.
